docs.title: Introduction
docs.text: • This datasheet documents the design of my individual subsystem for the Team 105 embedded systems project, from block diagram and component selection through schematic, power budget, PCB, and testing. It records the engineering decisions behind my portion of the system so it can be understood, reproduced, and evaluated.

docs.title: Project Summary
docs.text:
• Team 105 is developing RadioLink, a portable, off-grid communication device for when cellular or internet service is unavailable. Each team member builds one subsystem around a PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano, and the boards connect through standardized connectors with a shared ground.
  • My subsystem is audio input. A CMC-6027-24T electret microphone captures the user’s voice, and an MCP6004 amplifier stage boosts the signal for the PIC’s analog-to-digital converter. The board runs from a single 3.3 V supply.

docs.title: My Contribution
docs.text:
• I am responsible for the microphone subsystem: selecting the components, designing the amplifier circuit, and creating the schematic, PCB, power budget, and test features. The board includes a UART header, a pushbutton, and a test LED to support debugging.
  • The following sections cover the block diagram, component selection, bill of materials, schematic, power budget, PCB design, and verification results.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text: Microphone Input Block Diagram - The signal starts at a CUI Devices electret microphone. It’s small and cheap, but its output is only millivolts, so it goes into an MCP6004 op amp. I chose that op amp because it’s rail-to-rail, runs from 3.3 volts, and has four amplifiers in one chip, so I use one and have spares. The amplified signal goes to pin RA0, the ADC on the PIC18F57Q43, which turns sound into numbers. I send those numbers out over UART. I chose UART because it needs only TX, RX and ground, it’s built into the Curiosity Nano, and it connects straight to Sultan’s board through connector 1. I also have a push button on RC4 and a test LED on RA1.

docs.title: Component Selection
docs.text:
*Table 1: DAC Component Selection

Digital-to-Analog Converter (DAC) — Individual Subsystem

Solution Pros Cons Option 1. PIC18F57Q43 Internal 8-bit DACNo additional costLink to product * No additional cost* 8-bit output enough for speech* No SPI Communication required * No Dedicated High-Resolution Audio ADC* Limited Processing Horsepower for DSP* RAM Constraints for Audio Buffering * Option 2. * Texas Instruments DAC7512 * $7/each * Link to product * Excellent Audio Fidelity (12-Bit Resolution)* Rapid Serial Communication (Up to 30 MHz) * Glitch-Free Power-On Initialization * More expensive * No Breadboard-Friendly DIP Packages * Requires a Completely Custom Software Driver

Choice: Option 2: Texas Instruments DAC7512

Rationale: The PIC18F57Q43's internal 8-bit DAC is the best fit for this project. We already own the microcontroller board, so using its built-in peripheral adds no cost and no shipping or lead-time risk. Eight bits is sufficient for speech-quality audio, and the on-chip DAC removes the need for an SPI driver and extra wiring, which keeps both the firmware and the board layout simple. The DAC7512 would offer higher resolution (12-bit) and a buffered output, but that improvement is not needed for voice, and it would add cost, a custom driver, and delivery delays. The main tradeoff is a higher quantization noise floor, which is acceptable for this application.

Table 2: Microphone Component Selection

Microphone — Individual Subsystem

Solution Pros Cons * Option 1. * CUI Devices CMC-6027-24T Electret Microphone* Low cost (verify price)* Link to product * Low cost* Small 6 mm through-hole form factor* Analog output works directly with the PIC's ADC* Simple to prototype and solder * Output signal is very small and needs amplification* Needs a bias resistor and DC-blocking capacitor* Analog signal is susceptible to noise * Option 2. * Adafruit MAX9814 Microphone Amplifier Breakout* About $8/each (verify price)* Link to product * Built-in amplifier with automatic gain control* Higher output level, so less external circuitry* Ready to use on a breadboard * More expensive* Automatic gain control can distort or pump the audio* Hides the amplifier stage we are supposed to design

Choice: Option 1: CUI Devices CMC-6027-24T Electret Microphone

Rationale: The CMC-6027-24T is selected because it is inexpensive, small, and gives a plain analog signal that the PIC18F57Q43's ADC can read once it is amplified. Its output is small, so it pairs with the MCP6004 amplifier stage in the next table, and the extra bias and coupling components are cheap and easy to add. The MAX9814 breakout is more convenient, but it costs more and its built-in gain stage would replace the amplifier circuit that this subsystem is meant to design. The main tradeoff is added circuit complexity and noise sensitivity, which we address with proper decoupling and filtering before the ADC input.

Table 3: Amplifier Component Selection

Operational Amplifier — Individual Subsystem

Solution Pros Cons * Option 1. * Microchip MCP6004 Quad Op Amp* Low cost (verify price)* Link to product * Rail-to-rail input and output* Runs from 1.8 V to 6 V, compatible with the 3.3 V supply* Low power consumption* Spare op amps available for filtering * Gain-bandwidth of about 1 MHz limits very high gain* Four amplifiers in one package, so most go unused* Higher input noise than precision audio op amps * Option 2. * Texas Instruments LM358 Dual Op Amp* Low cost (verify price)* Link to product * Very common and easy to find* Through-hole DIP package is breadboard-friendly* Wide supply range * Output cannot swing to the positive rail* Poor performance at a 3.3 V supply* Higher power consumption

Choice: Option 1: Microchip MCP6004 Quad Op Amp

Rationale: The MCP6004 is selected because it operates from the same 3.3 V supply as the PIC18F57Q43 and has rail-to-rail input and output, so the amplified microphone signal can use the full 0 to 3.3 V range of the ADC. Its low power draw suits a small battery-style design, and the extra amplifiers in the package give us room to add a filter stage if needed. The LM358 is easier to find in a DIP package, but its output cannot reach the supply rails and it does not perform well at 3.3 V. The tradeoff is a modest gain-bandwidth product, which is more than enough for speech frequencies.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
Starting with power: a 9 volt barrel jack feeds an LM7805 regulator through a 1 amp fuse and a jumper (JP1) that lets me disconnect power. Capacitors on the regulator's input and output give a clean 5 volts. That feeds the Nano's VBUS pin. The Nano makes its own 3.3 volts, and I take that from the VTG pin to power the mic and op amp, so the signal can never go higher than the PIC's ADC can handle.

For the mic, a 2.2k resistor from 3.3 volts biases it. A 1 microfarad capacitor blocks DC and passes only the sound. Because I only have a single supply, I build a half-supply reference of about 1.65 volts, called VB, with two 10k resistors and a 10 microfarad capacitor. A 100k resistor ties the op amp input to VB.

The op amp is a non-inverting amplifier. A 47k feedback resistor and a 2.2k resistor in series with a 10 microfarad capacitor to ground give about 22 times gain on audio. DC passes at a gain of one, so the 1.65 volt center stays put. I wired the three unused amplifiers as buffers on VB, so they don't pick up noise.

The output goes through a 4.7k resistor and a 10 nanofarad capacitor. That's a low-pass filter at about 3.4 kilohertz, which protects RA0 and reduces aliasing at an 8 kilohertz sample rate.

The 8-pin header (J2) connects to Sultan's system: RX on pin 1 (RA1), TX on pin 2 (RB2), and ground on pin 8, matching our block diagram. Pins 3 through 7 are not connected. A second header (J4) breaks out spare GPIO (RC6, RD4, RA3, RA4) with 5 volts and ground. The (un)mute button on RC4 pulls the pin to ground, and the debugging LED on RC5 has a 300 ohm resistor. I added test points for 5 volts, 3.3 volts, ground, VB, MIC_OUT and ADC_IN, put no-connect flags on every unused pin, and ran KiCad's electrical rules check to catch mistakes.

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
A power budget was created to determine the current requirements of the microphone subsystem and verify that the selected power supply can safely support the complete circuit. The board uses a single 3.3 V power rail supplied by an external DC power supply, which provides the voltage directly to the circuit. Current requirements were estimated for the MCP6004 operational amplifier and the CMC-6027-24T electret microphone. The DAC is the PIC18F57Q43’s internal 8-bit DAC, so it is part of the microcontroller and does not add a separate load.

The estimated maximum current consumption of these components is approximately 0.9 mA. A 25% safety margin was added to account for variations in component current consumption and operating conditions, resulting in a design requirement of approximately 1.13 mA on the 3.3 V rail. This value was then compared with the 500 mA rating of the external power supply to verify that sufficient current capacity is available.

docs.title: Conclusions
docs.text:
The completed power budget indicates that the microphone subsystem can operate from a single 3.3 V power rail supplied by an external DC power supply. After applying the 25% safety margin, the calculated maximum current requirement is approximately 1.13 mA. The power supply is rated for up to 500 mA, leaving approximately 498.9 mA of current capacity beyond the calculated design requirement.

Because the subsystem draws only a small fraction of the available current, no additional voltage regulator is required. The CMC-6027-24T electret microphone represents the largest portion of the estimated current consumption, followed by the MCP6004 operational amplifier. The power budget demonstrates that the selected supply provides adequate current capacity, although the actual current consumption should be measured during subsystem verification to confirm the design estimates.
